questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Perpignan because it is in the South of France, and I love the area. I wanted to go on exchange to experience France and its culture, as well as utilising the language more. For these purposes, I felt that Southern France was perfect. So I can say that I chose my destination based on the food, culture, nature and weather.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My stay abroad was exceptional socially. I met some amazing people, and I got to experience some very cool and interesting things. I absolutely loved this aspect and would go back to the area in a heartbeat for this. However, my experience with the host university was not the best, but rather quite stressful. I didn't feel like I got the best reception as an Erasmus student, and the administration at the university was quite bad - I'm still having problems with attaining certain documents, and the pacing and quality of services simply don't live up to my own university. The problems I have experienced with administration have certanly tainted some aspects of my stay, so I would not recommend the univsersity itself to any future students.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was not very easy. I got my room and internet access easily. However, information about administrative things, such as attaining a student card, or finding out how to pay the rent was not given to me, and I had to get this information from former Erasmus students. Problems such as these also came when we had to inscribe to exams and get our grade transcripts - overall it wasn't easy, and one had to send many mails and proactively ask around a lot, to get the necessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was given a quick tour of the campus and a bunch of pamphlets about the area. Then I was given some information about what I needed to do, like getting room insurance or paying my deposit for the room. After this, not much assistance was offered.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I would have loved a better introduction to practical matters, as well as any kind of social introduction for foreign students. During my stay, the university didn't host an event of any kind, and students were left to socialize themselves. This worked out fine for most people, but some sort of meeting or any event hosted by the university would have helped and made the first few weeks easier and less lonely.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were single rooms available.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There were no meal plans and a shared kitchen. The kitchen didn't contain any cooking equipment, nor did it have any cupboards or an oven. This means that students have to buy everything they would need for cooking, and then store it in their rooms. This wasn't the worst but it would make cooking a bit complicated, as you probably have to walk back and forth between your room and the kitchen quite a bit while cooking.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The most important information is that the room has the necessary furniture (a bed, a desk, cupboards and a closet), but aside from that it is completely empty. So you need to be prepared to buy pillows, duvets and all necessary kitchen items for yourself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
My room was quite satisfactory, as I lived in one of the newer buildings. I was lucky, however, as some of the people living in the older dorms experienced a lot of noice, broken and faulty furniture and insects in their dorms. The quality of the housing will vary a lot depending on which building you get. However, the rooms all have the same overall structure.

It is a bit complicated to keep all kitchen appliances in your room, and there is only a small table in the kitchen. So there isn't much room for a larger group to eat together. Furthermore, there is no other area for the students to gather, so there isn't much opportunity for students to plan any kind of get-together. Since the campus is about 35 minutes from town (and therefore most bars and restaurants), it would have been nice to have some sort of area where people could meet - be it an empty room or just a room with a sofa or a large table. As it is now, the kitchens are shared by three corridors, and there is only a table that seats about four people - and the rooms are very small. So you don't have any opportunity to hang out in groups, unless you go into town, which is a real shame.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: We weren't given any information about when we had to register for courses, or how the university overall worked. But after a while, I found out that registration happened after three weeks, and before this, we were free to try out any courses available. This worked fine, but it would have been nice to get this information at the start.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
For three weeks you can visit any classes you're interested in, and then you should make a choice and let the professors know that you're joining the class. Later on, you sign up for the exams, which is a document that you fill out and get signed.

You should always let professors know that you're an Erasmus student who would like to follow the class so that they can add you manually. Also, some professors may not advise Erasmus students to follow their course, si it would be best to get it out of the way.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The necessary documentation is sent to you via email. It isn't totally clear how to fill it out, or who signs, but this can quickly be cleared up.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I filled out the necessary documentation and got it signed. After that I was registered for my exams, which wasn't too difficult.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You should definitely expect your courses to change after arrival. You will need to have around 10-12 courses, so many of your pre-chosen courses are likely to overlap on the schedule. Therefore you should be prepared to make some changes, will in turn will need to be approved by your university. This will give you some extra work.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level of courses is very different from universities in Denmark. Since you have 10-12 courses, they are all quite surface level. And be careful to choose the right courses upon your arrival, because not all of them can be recognised to be on a bachelor's level compared to Danish standards, which may cause you problems later on.
Overall, I found that the academic level was in many ways considerably lower than Danish standards - however, this varied a lot depending on the course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style is completely different. You aren't given much reading material but you will need to show up for class and listen to everything that is said (and take notes!!). because that is what is used for the exams. Also, the universities in France rely heavily on memorising what the professors say, and it isn't very analytical in nature. So it is important to show up, listen well and take notes.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I was enrolled in Latin, History of Contemporary Art, Linguistics, History of Rome, Comparative Literature, History of the French Langauge, Reflective Learning of a Language, Advanced German, Techniques of Expression in English, and then two French Erasmus courses.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend most literature courses, as they are easy to get approved by Danish universities, and I had some very good experiences with these courses - they had passionate teachers and interesting subject matter.
However, there may be problems with getting language courses approved in Denmark, as they may not live up to the Danish standard.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had no unexpected costs that I remember.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is very cheap compared to Denmark. You can also often find buses and train tickets for one euro (even longer trips). However, if you buy a cheap bike you won't need public transport much in your every day.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university had a lot of different classes for free, which was really cool!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university had a lot of different activities available, both creative and within sports. There were classes like pottery, sewing, drawing and singing, as well as football, volleyball, wrestling, yoga, and dancing. It was all free, you just had to sign up on a weekly basis.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend yoga, it was one of the few classes that I took, and it was extremely relaxing and nice.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would recommend visiting some of the smaller towns nearby, such as Carcasonne, Argeles-sur-mer, Banyuls-sur-mer, just generally some of the charming villages around. I would also recommend taking the two-hour bus to Barcelona, it is amazing. There are also really great hikes and cool things to see and experience in nature, such as big caves and natural hot springs.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The biggest cultural difference was the difference at the university, with classes and exams. However, you adjust quickly. Other than that I didn't find many cultural differences and absolutely love the French culture and mindset. It was easy to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to be the first to talk to someone. A lot of foreign students might think that the French students seem closed off or reserved, but they are extremely friendly and open to help - sometimes you just have to be the first one to talk.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't find that there were any challenging cultural differences (apart from systematic differences, like administrative difficulties or differences in university).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love the way the French know how to enjoy life and do a lot of different things on the weekends. They really know how to relax, enjoy food and enjoy life, without too much hurry and stress. I really appreciate this.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
I would say that you should be prepared for a lot of confusion around practical and administrative matters. Therefore, it is really important that you're not afraid to ask and send a lot of emails if you're ever in doubt about something. Don't be shy on that front.

Secondly, I would say that you should (probably) be prepared for a different university system than your own. At my own university class isn't mandatory, and there isn't too much time spent in class, but there is rather a lot of time spent on preparation. In France, it is mandatory to go to class, and you will most likely have a lot of classes to go to. It is really important that you go to class and listen well, as you aren't given much text or reading material, but the exams will be about what is said in class. Therefore, if you don't go to class, or you don't listen, you could lose a lot of valuable information that will be complicated to regain. Also, most exams are written exams, and they're done by hand - so you should get comfortable writing by hand for a long time.

Lastly, I would advise anyone to really enjoy and explore the area. Perpignan is close to Barcelona, Marseille, Montpellier and Toulouse - all great places! It is also close to the sea and the mountains, where you can go skiing in winter. It is a really amazing placement, where you can go and explore all kinds of different nature. I would highly advise anyone to explore the areas around and take advantage and travel while you're there.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
France offers a lot of student discounts, so always bring your student card when you're going somewhere. Also, the university offers a "culture pass", which will give you huge discounts on events, such as movie tickets, theatre, operas and all kinds of things like that.

Furthermore, the university has a lot of different free classes available. They offer a bunch of sports classes, like yoga, dancing, volleyball etc. (there are a lot!), and also a lot of creative classes, like singing, pottery, sewing and so on. Definitely take advantage of this, if you can.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part was definitely meeting so many amazing people and getting so many new friends. Throughout my stay, I also had to speak French the entire time, so it was probably the biggest improvement I have ever made with my language in such a short time.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The greatest challenge was definitely overcoming so many difficulties administratively. The university in France simply doesn't work on the same level as in Denmark. I don't mean to make too drastic statements, but getting things done and signed generally took ages, and things often had to be done twice due to mistakes. At the same time, the university of Perpignan often lacks satisfactory official documents, such as course descriptions and such, so there were a few times when documents had to be written and signed for a small matter.
I finished my exams in May, and I am still missing some key elements to finish my stay, so I recommend a lot of patience and perseverance when it comes to practical and administrative matters.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
